Very good collection of 6 HO games. I didn't play any of these games before so I was not familiar with these series. And as I can see from the reviews, people mostly prefer 1000 Doors and dislike Snark Busters. But I kinda liked Snark Busters. Yeah, the story in all 3 games is simple, I'd even say naive, but it has it's magic. These games also have beautiful and rather original visual style. Probably only All Revved Up is little weaker and lacks voiceacting.

As to the House of 1000 Doors... I'm not saying that they are bad, but I really liked only the first one - Family Secrets. Very grim and atmospheric game with really interesting story and good puzzles and mini games. The other two games have cool visuals and good atmosphere but the story is very lacking to say the least. Time travelling with mindless hopping from one setting to another - I've seen such vinaigrette in dozens of other similar games. And these 2 games are too easy.

But in the end - time well spent and overall impression is very good. If you are into hidden object game, it would be a good addition to your collection. Also, each House of 1000 Doors game has a bonus chapter. There are trading cards, achievements and for it's price, this collection offers more than enough.

Snark Buster:
The first time I played this game I was very excited by the way it handeled thing. For me, it was one of the first time that I played a non-traditional HOP game (Where you pick items from a list) here it was presented as you needed to find pieces to complete an item. Very nice.
The serie has a nice futuristic vibe thanks to the steam-punk theme. I love games that do something with mirror, stories or diving in people minds because it can create so much interesting worlds. You can clearly see that this is a game serie from the high days, when creative flew freely and the sky was the limit. Good game serie, nice memories.
One of the things that I didn't like about it was the lack of an end. i know with these kind of series open end is standard so more games can be made with the same idea. But the fact that we never even SAW the snark was a bit dissapointed. Then again, it was also the reason it keeps being a favorite of me. It remains a mysterie and because of the lact of an ending it is still strong.

House of 100 doors:
This is, by far, my favorite of the two series in this pack. I remember, as a kid, I tried to download as many 60-hour trial version to beat it however I can. So the first time I could play it fully is a very nice memory for me.
The cast of character is very good and there natural reactions are a sure add. The pleasant background and soft colors make the game nice for the eye.
However, there are also two big downsides for me.
The first is the fact that, however Samual says: You will meat the others residents later, we never actual see them. Even more, one of the main four (Being called Fleur in the dutch version) only appears once in the serie. I guess because she and Amanda furfill the same kind of role she was removed, but where Amanda has her artistic act (High lighted in Palm of Zoroaster) Fleur hardly has any deeper character beside being a medium. I might have liked seeing more residents (Truth, we do see Emily in Evil Inside but since that isn't in this pack I will ignore it) 
My second down point is the House itself. The first game really highlighted the house, where in the second and third game the focuss is more on the different worlds you travel to. Specially in the second game I feel this is an issue. The only real thing you see of the house are the painting hallway and the greenhouse you unlock later.
Even just the same rooms extended is fine. In the lore of the game itself the house provite everything needed for your quest, so I can't imagen thing like the Library in game one is only usefill because of the family tree. Or make a storyline where you go back to Amanda's workshop, now being restored. All those again can happen. 
Room for improvement, but just like with Snark, the fact it's open makes it a fine memory.

Update - I have now played the second and third "House of a Thousand Doors" and they are every bit as good, if not a bit better, than the original.  Just the usual HO game irritations like picky clicking and an few HO objects that don't match their description in the list.  

The House of Snark games are visually nice, great choice of music to set the mood, but the second one had a bug for me that rendered it unfinishable.  For the price one unplayable game out of six is not a big deal.  
The first House of Snark is good, really nice visuals, well chosen music, decent story.  I wish the items you have to find weren't so impossible to see sometimes.  They aren't full items, just parts so it can be a randomly shaped blip you're looking for in a very colorful and busy screen.  Luckily the hint button fills fast.  Also a number of the puzzles are quite poorly described as to how to go about doing what you're supposed to do so I skipped a number for sanity's sake.  For example, a puzzle where you had to link up a circuit by turning tiles to light all the bulbs, had a dead bulb sitting between two lit bulbs that it was literally connecting.
The second one, All Revved Up, was about the same until I hit a spot where I had to find three numbers, and I did.  I double checked and triple checked and went through walkthroughs and I have done everything right, but no matter what I do, it just keeps saying "wrong".   This is a progression puzzle (it is very clear where to find said numbers and I have done so) and is not a skippable one.  I will not be able to finish a game I paid to play.  As the game apparently randomly generates numbers on each new play-through I suspect there is a glitch, but I'm not about to start over.  There was another skippable puzzle too, that I solved but it would not give me the win.  I took a pic of my solution just to compare to the answer to see where I went wrong and the solutions are identical.  
I have played House of a Thousand Rooms in the past as an individual game and enjoyed it, just hope the other ones included here isn't a rush job to cash in on the name.

Old fashioned game with both Hidden object and 'adventure' (with inventory and puzzle solving). The graphics aren't great, but the play is still fun. The puzzles are pretty good, and there's an included hint-mode in each game that prevents frustration (although for experienced players, it's rarely needed). After 10 hours, I've solved 2 of the 6 games, which gives you an idea of the time needed to play. The story-line on the 1000 door is strongly occultic, which I"m not a fan of (in fact, all the games seem to focus on ghosts), but you can skip the cut scenes and the multitude of background written material (letters, newspaper articles, etc) scattered in the game world that might flesh out the story, but isn't necessary to solve the games. Overall, I enjoyed these and recommend them for someone looking for fun semi-casual play.

House of Snark 6-in-1 Bundle falls under the Hidden Object Adventure genre developed by Alawar Entertainment.

[h1] Gameplay / Story [/h1]

Snark Busters: Welcome to the Club: You join Kira Robertson on her search for the Snark, a deceptive and difficult-to-catch creature! Decipher clues, solve puzzles, combine objects and catch your opponent. Join the Snark Busters Club in this fast-paced and addicting hidden object game and follow the Snark through mirrors and upside-down worlds.

Snark Busters 2: Now at full throttle: And the hunt for the mysterious Snark continues. The club is also expecting a new member: Jack Blair. As a top racing driver, he was surprisingly invited to the club by his grandfather, who had actually disappeared, as the snark hunters suspect that he could be caught with a particularly fast sports car.

Don't much care for the House of Snark games, but the 1,000 Doors games are pretty fun.

SNARK BUSTERS:

All three are amazing games, although not proper HOGs.  These are called FROGs, FRactured Object Games.  Pieces of useful objects are scattered throughout each and every scene.  The locations of 80 to 90% of these fragments are pretty obvious once you let your eyes take in the scene.  The rest can pose a bit of a challenge to find.  Yet other fragments remain unavailable until certain actions are taken.  Once assembled, the objects enable you to manipulate things in the scene and advance the story.  Making changes in one scene, can lead to changes in another.  It can be quite a bit to keep track of as you are playing 5 or so scenes at the same time, but the game does usually prompt you.  Also, each scene has it's own inventory, so you are not walking around with dozens of fragments.

The mood is light and quirky.  The environment is cartoonish steampunk.  The music is upbeat.  There is no voiceover, the dialogue is all text. The tasks are engrossing and fun, even though the logic is a bit loose at times.  It took 3 to 4 hours to casually finish each installment, and I enjoyed almost every minute!

The first two, while generally easy, can pose a bit of a challenge at parts, but High Society does not.  Also, I never quite understood what I was meant to be doing when analyzing the photographs in that game.  I just kept clicking until it was accepted.  

By the way, I did get stuck on the T-Rex skeleton in the last part of Revved Up.  The Hint is of no help, but [spoiler] the sketch of your target pose is in the fireplace on the main floor [/spoiler] , which I completely missed.

Good hunting!

HOUSE OF 1,000 DOORS:

Stories of love and loss, apocalyptic devastation and redemption that you must resolve by finding items, solving puzzles and opening a lot of doors as you navigate a house with passageways to different times and dimensions.  Not 1,000 … but, still, a LOT. 

These games are quite complex.  Not complicated, per se, but there is a lot going on.  You have to juggle a lot of items in a lot of scenes.  They may not be as bright and pretty as Artifex games, but they do have their own fitting style and beauty.  And, at 5 to 6 hours each, they will keep you going for a lot longer than the newer HOGs.

Serpent Flame does try something new in having you put items into some of the hidden-object scenes rather than find them.  I can't say that I'm a fan, but at least it's different.

One caveat to these and other more complex HOGs is that if you leave them for a few days, it can be hard to regain the rhythm of what goes where.  Thank goodness for the interactive map!

OVERALL:

I heartily recommend that you give these games a go if you have the temperament and interest to seek out hidden objects in well-developed and engaging environments.  I had no issues running any of the 6 games on Windows 10.

These are good games for a good price. You should know that the games are actually bundled, as in, your 6 games don't appear separately, but as choices under a single menu, and that's how Steam reads them, in case this is important to you. To be fair, they did create achievements+cards for the bundle as a whole, so that's something at least.

That out of the way, this bundle has two different franchise sets in it, with the first three games of each, the first franchise being Snark Busters, the second House of 1000 Doors, and they're very different in both style and gameplay, though I personally enjoy both.
Snark is a lighthearted steampunk world in which there's, supposedly, a creature called a Snark that some people try to hunt, though it doesn't actually appear in the games and is mostly besides the point. The Snark world has an in-built bizarro world that you access via mirrors, and some actions taken on one side of the mirror affect things on the other side. I, personally, really enjoyed this aspect, though I can imagine it might get a bit confusing.
To cut down on the confusion, the items you need to use a room are only available there, and their fragments are found there, which brings me to the basics of Snark games, which is that it's overwhelmingly a fragmented object game, or, more accurately, lots of them, with a few easy puzzles/minigames thrown in. And when I say fragmented, I mean FRAGMENTED. As in, it's like all the items you need have exploded and scattered throughout each room/scene. It takes a minute to get used to it, but it's a lot of mindless, lighthearted fun, if you're into that sort of thing. The third game is the exception, in that each object or machine you need to fix has a wheel of items that are required to achieve that goal, and you click and drag them into that wheel, which conveniently pops up once you click on an item you've found (as well as showing you a gray image of the items you still need). The third game it also different in that it has more of a narrative to it with an actual overall goal. It's a significant improvement over the first two in terms of UI (the second game, for instance, stretches out if you want to play full screen, as if wide screen computers are a new invention or something, so that was annoying, and fixed in game 3), but I found the less farcical atmosphere, without the silly music, to be slightly less fun, but that's a personal thing.

House of 1000 Doors is entirely different, in terms of atmosphere, gameplay, and overall style. It's basically a mainstream hidden object/adventure game, with everything one comes to expect of the genre. The basic premise is there's a house that appears out of nowhere, and it has doors in it that are portals to different times and places, where you go around and try to fix what's bothering a restless ghost, which in turn affects the house and its residents. 
There are several of those tasks in each game, each including A LOT of standard hidden object scenes (as in, there's a list, you need to find items on it) as well as the standard variety of min-games/puzzles, and you do also have to collect items all over the place, which makes the interactive map very useful, especially later in the game when you've got a half dozen locks/puzzles/mini-games with parts missing and can't possibly remember which screw/bolt/figurine/fragment goes where). 
The doors to any particular time/place close once you've finished fixing what needed fixing, which cuts down on backtracking a little bit, though, since the games have collectible items, it means you can't go back if you missed one. 
The art is fine, the cut-scenes are mostly good, and the voice acting ranges from good to hilariously bad, but you can always skip if it bothers you. I've had no bugs.

Overall, it's very good value for money, if you like casual adventure HOG/FROG, and don't mind having your games bundled.

J'ai pris ce bundle en grosse promo car j'avais déjà 2 des House of 1000 doors, surtout pour House of 1000 doors The Serpents. Je n'ai pas été déçu. Il est dans la lignée de Family Secrets et Palm of Zoroastr que j'avais bien aimé (et que j'ai déjà évalués par ailleurs).  

House of 1000 doors The Serpents est un jeu du type aventure/objets cachés de bonne facture avec une histoire principale, un chapitre bonus consacré à un autre personnage, avec en bonus en plus des rejeux quelques fonds d'écran, et 4 puzzle supplémentaires. L'histoire est dans la veine fantastique usuelle du genre, avec une héroïne qui sauve le monde en se balladant dans l'espace-temps, en rencontrant des gens bizarres et en utilisant des objets bizarres. Pour peu que l'on ne soit pas trop regardant sur les détails ça coule plutôt bien. Fin du monde en approche oblige, on est dans une ambiance graphique plutôt terne sans être sinistre, avec des scènes suffisamment détaillées pour devoir rester attentif. L'intérêt du jeu est surtout dans ces énigmes mini-jeux et scènes d'objets cachés. L'aventure point&click est sans grande difficulté sans pour autant être trop directe. Il faudra parcourir plusieurs lieux pour la plupart des énigmes et en laisser certaines derrière un bon moment, mais vu qu'on dispose d'un journal assez précis et d'une carte avec transition rapide, ça se déroule bien sans jamais être pesant. Les mini-jeux ne sont pas bien durs non plus, du niveau simple coloriage à des équilibrages ou permutations un peu plus sophistiqués mais rien qui ne puisse se résoudre au pire en quelques tâtonnements. Ce qui m'a le plus résisté, et donc emballé, ce sont les SOC qui sont de 2 types : recherche d'objets pas nom ou placement d'objets dont on a le dessin. Avec souvent quelques animations du style écarter un rideau, regarder dans un tonneau, prendre un couteau et couper le pain avec... A noter la présence d'une collection d'objets métamorphes à collecter lors de l'aventure principale, seul point m'ayant déçu, je les ai trouvé trop en vue, la chasse ne prenait que quelques secondes.

A côté des House of 1000 doors les Snark Busters font pauvres mais ils m'ont agréablement surpris. "Bienvenue au club" et "Sur les chapeaux de roues" sont des jeux de recherches de d'objets par fragments. Il n'y a pas de scénes spécifiques aux objets cachés, les petits bouts sont répartis dans le décor et une fois les objets reconstitués on les utilise façon point&click. Ces 2 jeux n'ont pas vraiment d'histoire, juste un point de départ ensuite on passe d'un lieu à un autre sans autre but que de finir ces énigmes. Il y a quand même de courts épisodes narratifs quand on tombe sur une télé et qu'on y regarde les infos, c'est sans grand intérêt mais assez fun comme présentation de la trame. Ces jeux sont dans le style cartoon bien flashy. Donc le coeur des Snark Busters est la recherche de fragments d'objets. Et si c'est intellectuellement peu satisfaisant et gratifiant de chercher un bout de truc qui ne ressemble à rien, c'est assez redoutable en terme de capacité d'observation. Parce que ça peut aller de l'éclat de verre rouge sur une pelouse bien verte, qui se voit instantanément comme un nez de clown, au bout de bois marron issu d'un manche de marteau incrusté dans une rampe en bois marron aussi  qui va faire pleurer nos petits yeux un bon moment. 
"Haute société" est assez différent. Tout d'abord il y a une histoire, pas très développée mais qui rythme les changements de lieux du jeu. Et surtout on va chercher souvent de vrais objets, qui par groupes thématiques de 5, permettent d'agir sur un élément du décor. Par exemple pour réparer un évier il faudra trouver un robinet, ses têtes, une bonde et je ne sais plus quoi parfois dans plusieurs pièces.
Dans les 3 Snark Busters il m'est arrivé assez souvent d'être un peu perdu car on se retrouve vite avec beaucoup d'actions en parallèles réparties sur plusieurs lieux et qui interagissent entre elles. A ces moments là, l'absence de carte se fait cruellement sentir. Entre les lieux réels et les lieux miroirs c'est vite le labyrinthe.
A noter un gros désagrément avec la VF des Snark Busters. "Sur les chapeaux de roue" et "Haute société" n'affiche aucun caractère accentué et loupe aussi les ç. Lire "ct" et comprendre "à côté" ne m'est pas franchement naturel.
